Agribot recognises 8 tomato leaf conditions (early blight, late blight, leaf miner, magnesium, nitrogen and potassium deficiency, spotted wilt virus) and healthy leaves, and says when a problem is not one of these. It works fully offline; photos never leave your phone. Results are guidance only and can be wrong — always confirm with your local agriculture officer or Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) before treating plants.
Point your phone at tomato leaves. Agribot finds the leaves, checks each one and gives a single answer for the plant.

• Hold the phone 20–40 cm from the leaves
• Use daylight; avoid strong shadows
• Hold steady for a few seconds
• Show several leaves, including lower ones
Agribot can be wrong. Before spraying anything, confirm with your local agriculture officer or Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK).
Brown spots with rings, like a target, on older lower leaves, often with yellowing around them. A fungus that spreads in warm, wet weather.
Remove badly spotted lower leaves and destroy them away from the field. Do not leave them on the ground.
Water at the base of the plant, not on the leaves, preferably in the morning.
Keep space between plants for air flow and mulch the soil so it does not splash onto leaves.
Next season, do not plant tomato, potato or brinjal in the same place.
Large dark, water-soaked patches that spread fast, sometimes with white growth underneath in damp weather. It can destroy a crop within days.
Act quickly: remove infected leaves or plants, bag them and destroy them. Do not compost them.
Tell your agriculture officer or KVK and nearby farmers — late blight spreads between fields.
Keep leaves dry and improve air flow between plants.
Check the rest of the field every day while the weather stays cool and wet.
Winding pale tunnels or blotches inside the leaf, made by small insect larvae feeding between the leaf surfaces.
Pick off and destroy leaves with tunnels.
Use yellow sticky traps to watch for the adult insects.
Check the undersides of leaves often. Ask your KVK about pheromone traps if tomato leaf miner (Tuta absoluta) is in your area.
Yellowing between the veins of older leaves while the veins stay green.
Get a soil test before adding any fertiliser.
Ask your agriculture officer which magnesium source and amount suit your soil.
Sandy or acidic soils and heavy potash use make this more likely.
Older leaves turn evenly pale green to yellow and the plant grows slowly.
Add well-rotted compost or farmyard manure.
Ask your agriculture officer for the right fertiliser dose for your soil and crop stage.
Yellow, then brown and dry edges on older leaves. Fruit may ripen unevenly.
Ask your agriculture officer for the right potassium source and dose.
Keep soil moisture even; very dry or waterlogged soil makes it worse.
Bronze or purple spots and rings on young leaves; plants may be stunted. A virus spread by thrips (tiny insects). There is no cure.
Remove and destroy infected plants to protect the rest.
Clear weeds around the field — they shelter thrips and the virus.
Use blue or yellow sticky traps to watch for thrips.
Ask your KVK about resistant varieties for the next season.
No signs of the 8 conditions on the leaves that were checked.
Keep checking every week, especially after rain.
Look at the lower leaves too — problems often start there.
The leaves do not look healthy, but they do not match any condition this app knows (for example bacterial spot, leaf mould, mosaic virus or septoria leaf spot).
Show the plant, or a clear photo, to your agriculture officer or KVK.
Keep sick-looking plants apart from healthy ones until you know more.
Do not spray anything until the problem is identified.
